claims.text: The single-crystal FeNiCrCoCu coating initially has a stable FCC crystalline structure.
The FeNiCrCoCu coating has a low dislocation density at 300 K.
At 300–600 K, dislocation density decreases while the lattice remains crystalline.
The crystalline condition at 300–600 K maintains higher hardness and lower friction than the condition above 900 K.
Above 900 K, thermally activated stacking-fault annihilation occurs in the FeNiCrCoCu coating.
Thermal energy above 900 K exceeds the stacking-fault energy barrier.
Annihilation of Shockley partial dislocations causes dislocation starvation.
Stacking-fault annihilation and dislocation starvation trigger localized amorphization in FeNiCrCoCu above 900 K.
In nanocrystalline CoCrFeNiMn with a 2.0 nm grain size, amorphization obscures melting.
Localized amorphization eliminates the dislocation sources required for plastic flow.
The resulting amorphous layer has low shear strength.
Reduced shear resistance promotes severe adhesive wear and material transfer.
Adhesive material transfer causes the coefficient of friction to spike.
The coefficient of friction and wear rate increase sharply above 900 K.
Above 900 K, the FCC phase fraction decreases while HCP or amorphous atom counts increase in the contact zone.
Above 900 K, total dislocation line length falls to near zero because of dislocation starvation.
Mechanical annealing would preserve crystalline order rather than produce amorphization.
High dislocation line length above 900 K would indicate mechanical annealing rather than dislocation starvation.
Grain-boundary sliding dominates deformation in nanocrystalline variants of this alloy system.
Below 900 K, dislocation-mediated deformation remains viable.

contradictions.description: The proposed sequence requires stacking-fault annihilation, but the predicted signature permits a rise in HCP atom count, which commonly represents stacking-fault or partial-dislocation structures. No formation of new HCP defects after annihilation is specified to reconcile these statements.

Mechanical annealing is described as preserving crystalline order, but high dislocation line length is separately declared an indicator of mechanical annealing. The relationship between retained crystallinity, annealing, and high versus reduced dislocation density is not made internally consistent.
